_comment: AQA 8700 skills pages: language analysis, comparing viewpoints, planning, common mistakes, revision. Marks and AO references verified from AQA's specification, scheme of assessment and specimen mark schemes. All extracts, practice tasks and model answers are original RCF English work.

pages.title: Language Analysis Techniques
pages.metaTitle: GCSE Language Analysis: How to Write About Effect | RCF English
pages.description: How to analyse language for AQA GCSE English Language: what to notice, which terms to use, and how to write about effect instead of spotting techniques.
pages.keywords: GCSE language analysis, how to analyse language GCSE, language techniques GCSE English, AQA language question, writing about effect GCSE

hero.text: The mark is not for naming the technique. It is for explaining what the technique does to a reader - which is why a student who knows twenty terms can still be stuck in the middle band.

blocks.title: About the examples on this page
text: Every extract, example and practice task here was written by RCF English. They are **not** AQA questions or AQA source texts, and no AQA mark scheme wording is reproduced. RCF English is not affiliated with, endorsed by or approved by AQA.
AQA's own specimen papers, mark schemes and examiner reports are linked on the [papers page](global-english/gcse/aqa/papers/) and are the authoritative guide to the standard.

blocks.text: **Language analysis is assessed by AO2 on both papers: Paper 1 Question 2 (8 marks) and Paper 2 Question 3 (12 marks).** AQA's objective asks you to explain, comment on and analyse how writers use language to achieve effects and influence readers, using relevant subject terminology. Every word in that sentence matters, and *terminology* is the last one, not the first.

blocks.title: The one sentence that changes most answers
text: **Do not ask what technique this is. Ask what changes for the reader because the writer chose this word instead of a near-synonym.**

*The wind was strong* and *the wind was relentless* are both descriptions of wind. The second adds duration and a hint of intention. That difference - which needs no technical term at all - is what AO2 rewards.

blocks.heading: What to notice, in order of usefulness

parts.heading: 1. Verbs
text: The most under-used evidence at GCSE. Verbs carry force, speed and intention. *The frost had taken the field* makes the frost an invader; *the frost had covered the field* makes it weather.

parts.heading: 2. Unexpected pairings
text: A word that does not usually belong with its neighbour is always deliberate. *A resentful relationship with rain* attaches an emotion to weather and a grudge to the writer, in four words.

parts.heading: 3. Sentence length and shape
text: A short sentence after long ones lands. A very long sentence can enact tiredness, accumulation or panic. Sentence forms are one of the three bullet prompts AQA prints under its Paper 1 language question, so they are explicitly invited.

parts.heading: 4. What is repeated
text: Repetition is easy to spot and easy to explain: it tells you what the writer will not let you forget.

parts.heading: 5. What is withheld
text: Absence is evidence. A description with no colour in it, a narrator who never names a feeling, a passage where nobody speaks - all are choices.

blocks.heading: Terms worth knowing, and what to say about each

items.definition: A comparison using like or as. Say what quality is being transferred, and whether it is a surprising choice.
items.example: "pale as bone" transfers not only colour but hardness and death.

items.definition: A comparison stated as fact. Ask what the writer gains by not saying like.
items.example: Calling silence a weight makes it something the character carries.

items.definition: Giving human qualities to something that is not human. Say what relationship it creates.
items.example: A barn that is nearer "than it had any right to be" is being accused of misbehaving.

items.definition: A group of words from the same area of meaning running through a passage. Useful because it is about the whole extract, not one word.
items.example: Words of measurement and distance running through a passage about disorientation.

items.definition: Repeated s sounds. Only worth naming if you can say what it does here - it is not automatically soothing or sinister.
items.example: Say why the softness suits this moment, or do not mention it.

items.definition: A flat statement. Naming the sentence type is worth a mark only with the effect attached.
items.example: "The distances were wrong." Four words, no hedging, so the reader accepts it as Martha does.

items.definition: Two contrasting things placed side by side. Say what the contrast exposes.
items.example: Better calves set beside a resentful relationship with rain, so the physical gain looks small.

blocks.heading: The four-move paragraph
text: Every language paragraph that reaches the top band does these four things, in this order. The fourth is the one most answers stop before.
numbered: **Quote** briefly, embedded in your own sentence.
**Identify** what the writer is doing - with a term if you are sure of it, in plain words if not.
**Develop** - a second reading of one word, or a link to how it works with something else in the extract.

blocks.heading: The same quotation, at three levels

items.label: Original RCF example: "the frost had taken the field entirely"
items.prompt: How does the writer use language to describe the frost?
sample: **Lower band.** The writer uses the word "taken" which is a powerful verb. This shows that the frost is strong. It makes the reader imagine the frost.

**Middle band.** The writer uses the verb "taken", which suggests the frost has captured the field like an army. The adverb "entirely" shows that no part of the field has escaped, which makes the frost seem powerful and total.

**Top band.** The verb "taken" turns weather into occupation: the frost does not settle on the field, it takes possession of it, and the field becomes territory rather than ground. "Entirely" then closes off any exception, so the reader is given no corner of the scene to feel safe in. The choice matters most because a near-synonym would have done neither - "covered" would have left the field underneath, still itself, waiting.
notes: The lower-band answer names a feature and asserts an effect. *Powerful verb* is a label, and *makes the reader imagine* is true of all writing.
The middle-band answer explains a real effect and uses terms accurately. It stops after the explanation - which is where most competent answers stop.

The top-band answer does one extra thing: it compares the writer's choice with the choice not made. That single move - *a near-synonym would have done neither* - is the clearest route from middle to top, and it needs no additional terminology.

blocks.heading: Practice, and mark your own
text: **Original RCF practice task.** Take any paragraph of description from a novel you own. Write one four-move paragraph about a single verb in it. Then check:
items: Is my quotation short enough to sit inside my own sentence?
Have I said what the effect is on a **reader**, not what the word means?
Have I named a technique only where I am certain of the term?
Have I compared the writer's choice with a plainer alternative?
Could this paragraph have been written about any text? If so, it is too general to earn marks.

items.q: Do I lose marks for not using technical terms?
a: AQA's objective asks for relevant subject terminology, so terms are part of it - but they are one part of four, alongside explaining, commenting and analysing. A precise explanation with no term scores better than a term with a vague explanation, and a term used wrongly is worse than no term at all.

items.q: How many techniques should I identify?
a: Three developed points for the 8-mark question and four for the 12-mark question is a reliable shape. The specimen mark schemes reward a judicious range of examples rather than a long list, so depth beats coverage.

items.q: What if I cannot see any techniques in the extract?
a: Then write about the words themselves. Verbs, unexpected pairings, sentence length and repetition are present in every passage and need no special vocabulary to discuss. Extracts chosen for this question always reward attention; they do not always contain similes.

pages.title: Comparing Writers' Viewpoints
pages.metaTitle: GCSE Comparing Writers' Viewpoints: AQA Paper 2 Question 4 | RCF English
pages.description: How to compare writers' viewpoints for AQA English Language Paper 2 Question 4: the paragraph shape, the connectives, and a worked comparison worth 16 marks.
pages.keywords: comparing writers viewpoints, AQA paper 2 question 4, GCSE comparison question, how to compare two sources GCSE, AO3 GCSE English

hero.text: Sixteen marks, one question, and one rule that fixes most answers: never write a paragraph about only one of the two writers.

blocks.title: About the examples on this page
text: The worked comparison below uses two original sources written by RCF English. They are **not** AQA sources, and no AQA mark scheme wording is reproduced. RCF English is not affiliated with, endorsed by or approved by AQA.
AQA's own specimen papers and mark schemes are linked on the [papers page](global-english/gcse/aqa/papers/).

blocks.text: **AQA Paper 2 Question 4 is worth 16 marks and assesses AO3: compare writers' ideas and perspectives, as well as how these are conveyed, across two or more texts.** The objective has two halves - *what* they think and *how* they show it - and both are marked. It is the only question on either paper that assesses AO3.

blocks.heading: Why most answers lose marks here
bullets: **They summarise instead of comparing.** Two paragraphs describing Source A, then two describing Source B, with the word *however* between them. The examiner has to do the comparing.
**They compare attitudes but not methods**, or methods but not attitudes. Half the objective, half the marks.
**They rank the writers.** *Source A is better written* is not a comparison of perspectives.
**They run out of time.** It is the last question in Section A and it is worth the most.

blocks.heading: The paragraph shape that fixes it

items.title: Name the difference
text: Open with the point of difference itself, not with a writer. *The two writers differ most in how certain they allow themselves to sound.*

items.title: Writer A: attitude, then method
text: A short quotation, what it shows about the attitude, and how the writing conveys it.

items.title: Writer B: attitude, then method
text: The same, connected explicitly - *where the first writer asserts, the second concedes*.

items.title: Weigh them
text: One sentence judging the effect: which is more forceful, more convincing, more honest, and why. This is the sentence that separates the top band.

items.definition: Puts both writers in one sentence and makes the contrast structural.
items.example: Where the first writer states, the second admits.

items.definition: Simple, clear, and signals a genuine turn.
items.example: By contrast, the modern writer refuses the claim entirely.

items.definition: Useful when the attitudes agree and only the methods differ.
items.example: Both value solitude, but one commands and the other confides.

items.definition: Best used mid-sentence, joining two clauses of equal weight.
items.example: The 1871 writer measures thinking in miles, whereas the columnist measures it in interruptions avoided.

items.definition: The weighing move. Rarely used and always rewarded.
items.example: This is more persuasive because she has already conceded her case is small.

items.label: Original RCF example, using the two walking sources
items.prompt: Compare how the two writers convey their different attitudes to what walking is worth. (The two sources are on the [Paper 2 questions page](global-english/gcse/aqa/paper-2/questions/) and are original RCF passages, not AQA sources.)
sample: The two writers disagree most about whether walking improves the person doing it. The 1871 writer treats it as a discipline with measurable results, claiming that "the quality of a man's thinking may be measured tolerably well by the number of miles he has walked alone". The verb "measured" is doing the persuasive work: it borrows the language of science for what is really a preference, and the calm qualifier "tolerably well" makes the claim sound cautious when it is in fact enormous. By contrast the modern writer denies any improvement at all - "I did not have profound thoughts. Mostly I thought about lunch" - and conveys her attitude through anticlimax, setting up the expectation of insight in one sentence and puncturing it in the next. Where the first writer builds authority by sounding measured, the second builds it by sounding unimpressed with herself, and hers is the more persuasive method for a modern reader precisely because she has removed the motive for exaggeration.

They also differ in what they think walking gives back. For the older writer the gain is knowledge of a place got "by the body as well as the mind", a phrase whose balanced structure quietly presents a personal belief as an established distinction. For the columnist the gain is nothing to do with knowledge; it is "a stretch of the day that nobody could book a meeting in", where the intrusion of workplace vocabulary into a description of freedom conveys exactly what she is escaping. The older writer therefore argues for walking as an addition to a life, while the younger argues for it as a subtraction from one - and the subtraction is the more vivid case, because the reader recognises the meetings.
notes: **Both writers appear in every paragraph.** Neither paragraph could be split in half without collapsing.
**Attitude and method are handled together**, not in separate sentences: the attitude is named, then the writing that conveys it is analysed in the same breath.
**Each paragraph ends by weighing.** *Hers is the more persuasive method ... precisely because* is the AO3 sentence that most answers omit.
**Quotations are short.** Nothing longer than a clause, all embedded, which leaves room for analysis in a 20-minute answer.
**No ranking of quality.** The comparison is about perspective and method, never about which writer is better.

blocks.heading: Practice, then check
text: **Original RCF practice task.** Using the same two sources, compare how the two writers convey their different attitudes to the opinions of other people. Three paragraphs, about 20 minutes. Then check:
items: Does every paragraph contain both writers?
Have I named an attitude before analysing any method?
Have I used a comparative connective in every paragraph?
Have I weighed the two writers at least once?
Have I avoided saying that one writer is simply better?
Have I quoted briefly enough to leave room for analysis?

items.q: Should I compare attitudes or methods?
a: Both, in the same paragraphs. AO3 asks you to compare writers' ideas and perspectives *as well as how these are conveyed*, so an answer that does only one of the two has met half the objective and will be capped accordingly.

items.q: How many points of comparison do I need?
a: Three developed points, each in its own paragraph, is a full answer for 16 marks in about 20 minutes. Two very well developed points can also reach the top band; five thin ones will not.

items.q: What if the two writers largely agree?
a: Then compare how they agree. Two writers can hold the same view and convey it in entirely different ways - one through anecdote and one through statistics, one warmly and one angrily - and that is a legitimate and often high-scoring comparison.

pages.title: Planning and Structuring Answers
pages.metaTitle: How to Plan GCSE English Language Answers | RCF English
pages.description: Paragraph shapes and planning methods for every question on AQA GCSE English Language, with the time each plan should take and what it protects.
pages.keywords: how to plan GCSE English answers, GCSE English paragraph structure, PEE paragraph GCSE, AQA English Language planning, structuring GCSE English answers

hero.text: Ten questions across two papers, and five different paragraph shapes between them. Knowing which shape a question wants is worth more than any amount of extra reading.

blocks.title: About the examples on this page
text: The before-and-after example below was written by RCF English and is not taken from an AQA paper or mark scheme. Marks and timings are AQA's; the paragraph shapes are RCF recommendations. RCF English is not affiliated with, endorsed by or approved by AQA.

blocks.text: **Every question on AQA English Language has a shape that suits it, and using the wrong shape is the most common structural error at GCSE.** A structure answer written as language analysis, or a comparison written as two summaries, loses marks that the student had the material to earn.

blocks.heading: Which shape for which question
blocks.caption: Planning times are RCF recommendations within AQA's published section timings.
rows: Four short answers. No paragraphs at all.
Three paragraphs: quote, identify, explain, develop
Beginning, shift, end, plus one running feature
Difference, quote A, quote B, inference - repeated
Four paragraphs: quote, identify, explain, develop twice
Position, then four paragraphs, one of them a qualification
Three paragraphs, both writers in each, weighing at the end
Five or six paragraphs with a deliberate shape and a chosen ending

blocks.heading: What a plan is actually for
text: A plan is not a summary of what you are going to say. It is a decision about **order** and about **where you will stop**. Those are the two things students lose under time pressure, and they are the two things the content and organisation marks are looking at.

parts.heading: For a reading question
text: Three or four quotations, listed in the order you will use them, with one word beside each saying what it is for. That is the whole plan. It takes under a minute and it stops you writing three paragraphs about your best quotation and none about the rest of the extract.

parts.heading: For a writing question
text: Your last line, written first. Then three or four things that must happen before it. Knowing the destination is what prevents the drift that costs organisation marks in the fourth paragraph.

blocks.heading: Beyond point-evidence-explain
text: Most students arrive at GCSE with a three-part paragraph: point, evidence, explanation. It is a reasonable floor and a low ceiling, because it stops exactly where the higher bands begin. Two additions convert it.
bullets: **A fourth move: develop.** After explaining the effect, take one word further - a second reading, or a comparison with the plainer word the writer did not use.
**A zoom.** Quote a phrase, then requote two words of it. *"pale as bone" - and "bone" rather than "paper", so the hardness comes with the colour.*
**For comparison questions, a fifth move: weigh.** One sentence judging which writer's method is more effective and why.

blocks.heading: The same point, before and after

items.label: Original RCF example
items.prompt: Adding the fourth move to a standard three-part paragraph.
sample: **Three moves.** The writer describes the frost as "pale as bone". This is a simile. It suggests the field looks dead and colourless, which creates a bleak atmosphere for the reader.

**Four moves.** The writer describes the frost as "pale as bone". The simile brings death into a description of weather, so the field is not merely cold but lifeless, and the bleakness arrives before any character does. The choice of "bone" rather than a comparison with paper or with snow is what makes it work: bone is hard as well as pale, so the simile carries the surface's brittleness and its colour in a single word.
notes: The three-move version is accurate and would earn marks. It ends at the effect.
The four-move version does one extra thing - it names the alternative the writer rejected, and shows what that choice bought. It is about forty words longer.
This is the cheapest available improvement in the whole paper. It requires no additional reading, no additional terminology and no additional quotation.

blocks.heading: Planning checklist
items: Have I identified which **kind** of question this is before choosing a shape?
For reading: have I listed my quotations in the order I will use them?
For writing: do I know my last line before I write my first?
Have I decided where to stop, so the final question still has its time?
Have I planned a qualification for Question 4 on Paper 1, and a weighing sentence for Question 4 on Paper 2?

pages.title: Common Student Mistakes
pages.metaTitle: AQA GCSE English Language: Common Mistakes to Avoid | RCF English
pages.description: The mistakes that cost the most marks on AQA GCSE English Language, question by question, and what to do instead.
pages.keywords: GCSE English Language common mistakes, AQA English Language mistakes, why students lose marks GCSE English, GCSE English exam errors

hero.text: Almost none of these are mistakes of knowledge. They are mistakes of habit, which means they can be fixed in a fortnight.

blocks.text: **The marks lost most often on this qualification are not lost because a student did not understand the text.** They are lost by answering a different question from the one asked, by running out of time, or by stopping a paragraph one move too early.

parts.heading: Answering from the wrong lines
text: Paper 1 Questions 1 and 2 and Paper 2 Question 1 all name specific lines. Material from elsewhere in the source earns nothing, however good it is. **Fix:** underline the line numbers before reading the question again.

parts.heading: Analysing the wrong source
text: Paper 2 Question 3 names one source. Students who have just spent Question 2 working across both sometimes carry on. **Fix:** circle the source letter in the question.

parts.heading: Writing the wrong form
text: A speech submitted where a letter was asked for loses part of AO5, which covers adapting to form, purpose and audience. **Fix:** write the form and the audience at the top of your planning space before you plan anything else.

parts.heading: Running out of time for Section B
text: Section B is 40 marks, exactly as many as the whole reading section. A student who gives it twenty minutes has capped their grade before writing a word. **Fix:** treat 45 minutes for Section A as a hard stop, even mid-sentence.

blocks.heading: Reading questions
do: Q1: four short phrases, then stop.
Q2 and P2 Q3: three or four quotations, each developed to a second reading.
P1 Q3: write about order, focus and shift - the shape of the whole extract.
P1 Q4: state a position in sentence one and qualify it once.
P2 Q4: both writers in every paragraph, weighed at the end.
dont: Do not write full sentences for Question 1, or give five answers.
Do not list techniques - *there is a simile, there is alliteration* - without effect.
Do not answer P1 Q3 with language analysis. It is the commonest single error on Paper 1.
Do not sit on the fence for twenty marks. *To some extent* with nothing after it is not evaluation.
Do not write about Source A, then Source B, with *however* in between.

blocks.heading: Writing questions
do: Plan for five minutes and check for five.
Vary sentence length deliberately, including one very short sentence at a turning point.
Use punctuation you can use accurately.
Write about something you can picture or have an opinion about.
Keep one line of argument, or one shape, from start to finish.
dont: Do not open a story with an alarm clock, and do not end one with waking up.
Do not reach for long words you cannot spell - accuracy is 16 of the 40 marks.
Do not invent statistics in a viewpoint piece; specific real detail persuades further.
Do not string rhetorical devices together as a checklist.
Do not add a twist to what the paper called *the opening part* of a story.

blocks.title: The most expensive habit of all
text: Stopping a paragraph after the explanation. A student who writes *this creates a bleak atmosphere for the reader* and moves on has done everything the middle band asks and nothing the top band asks.

The fix takes one sentence: say why **that** word rather than the plainer one the writer could have used. See the before-and-after example on [planning and structuring answers](global-english/gcse/aqa/planning-answers/).

blocks.heading: A two-minute check before you hand the paper in
items: Did I answer Question 1 from the right lines, with exactly four things?
Did I write about **structure** in Paper 1 Question 3, not language?
Did I take a clear position in Paper 1 Question 4?
Does every paragraph of Paper 2 Question 4 contain both writers?
Is my Section B piece in the form and for the audience the task named?
Did I spend the last five minutes checking spelling, punctuation and sentence boundaries?

pages.title: Revision Strategies
pages.metaTitle: How to Revise GCSE English Language: AQA 8700 | RCF English
pages.description: How to revise AQA GCSE English Language when there are no set texts: what to practise, how often, and a six-week plan that fits around other subjects.
pages.keywords: how to revise GCSE English Language, AQA English Language revision, GCSE English revision plan, revising English Language with no texts

hero.text: There is nothing to memorise, which is why students find this the hardest subject to revise and the easiest to neglect. What you are practising is a set of moves.

blocks.text: **Every source in both AQA English Language papers is unseen, so revision cannot mean learning content.** It means rehearsing five things until they are automatic: reading a question accurately, choosing quotations quickly, developing a point past the explanation, holding a shape in a piece of writing, and keeping to time.

parts.heading: 1. The four-move paragraph, five minutes at a time
text: Open any book. Take one sentence. Write one paragraph: quote, identify, explain, develop. Five minutes, three or four times a week, does more for the language questions than an hour of reading revision notes.

parts.heading: 2. Timed single questions
text: Do not always do whole papers. A single 20-minute Question 4 is easier to fit into an evening, and it is the question worth the most reading marks. Whole papers are for the last fortnight.

parts.heading: 3. Openings, over and over
text: Write the first 150 words of a description or a story twice a week. Not the whole thing - the opening. Openings are what the examiner meets first, and they are the part most improved by repetition.

parts.heading: 4. Reading non-fiction with a pen
text: For Paper 2, read one opinion column a week and write two sentences: what the writer's attitude is, and one thing in the writing that conveys it. That is the whole of Question 3 and half of Question 4, practised in five minutes.

parts.heading: 5. Accuracy drills
text: Sixteen of the forty writing marks are technical accuracy. Take a piece you have written, and check it for one thing only - sentence boundaries this time, apostrophes next time. Checking for everything at once finds nothing.

blocks.heading: A six-week plan
blocks.caption: About three hours a week. Adjust the balance towards whichever paper you find harder.
rows: P1 Q4: taking a position and qualifying
P2 Q2 and Q3: summary and the 12-mark language question
P2 Q4: both writers in every paragraph
One full Paper 1 and one full Paper 2, to time

blocks.title: Mark your own work against the real thing
text: AQA publishes specimen and past mark schemes, and its examiner reports say plainly what candidates did badly that year. Both are free and linked on the [papers page](global-english/gcse/aqa/papers/).
Read one examiner report before you next sit a practice paper. It is the most direct account available of where marks actually go, and almost no student reads one.

blocks.heading: Signs your revision is working
items: You can name the question type from the wording, without being told.
You choose quotations in under a minute rather than rereading the whole extract.
Your paragraphs have four moves, not three, without you thinking about it.
You finish Section A in 45 minutes and start Section B without panic.
You know, before you write a story, what its last line will be.
Your accuracy check finds two or three real errors, not none.

items.q: How do I revise English Language when there is nothing to learn?
a: By practising moves rather than memorising content. The five worth practising are: reading the question accurately, selecting quotations quickly, developing a point past the explanation, holding a shape in a piece of writing, and keeping to time. Short, frequent practice beats long sessions, because these are habits rather than facts.

items.q: Should I do whole past papers?
a: In the last two or three weeks, yes. Before that, single timed questions are more useful: they are easier to fit in, easier to mark honestly, and they let you work on the specific question that is costing you marks rather than rehearsing the ones you already do well.

items.q: Does reading novels improve my grade?
a: It improves the raw material - vocabulary range, sentence variety, a feel for how a paragraph is built - which shows up in the 40-mark writing questions. It does not by itself teach you the question methods, and it is slower than practice. Do both, and do not let reading substitute for timed writing.

items.q: How much writing practice is enough?
a: Two short openings a week and one full 45-minute piece a fortnight is realistic alongside other subjects. The writing questions are worth 80 of the 160 marks on this qualification, so they deserve at least half your English Language revision time - which is roughly double what most students give them.
